judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET 10 on Linux with root access and native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly matches the requested .NET/Linux collection workflow, gives usable collect-linux commands, and explains its perf_events/native-stack value. It omits the requested fallback guidance, but A misses the central recommended tool and command altogether.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET Framework on Windows without admin privileges
judgeRationales.rationale: B accurately centers the decisive .NET Framework limitation: effective CPU tracing via PerfView requires admin access, dotnet-trace is not applicable, and dumps are only a limited fallback. A includes several misleading or overbroad claims and omits PerfView, so it could lead the user toward ineffective collection.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assembly loading failure on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B is focused on the appropriate assembly-loader EventPipe collection and, crucially, covers tracing from process launch. Its illustrative DLL launch command may need `dotnet` before a DLL unless an executable apphost is used, but it is still substantially more useful for the stated startup scenario. A has a plausible provider command and useful LoaderExceptions advice, but misses the key startup collection method and includes questionable unrelated environment-variable suggestions.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly and correctly answers the requested SDK-free acquisition path with an appropriate command and collection example. A omits that path and includes substantial technical inaccuracies, such as treating dotnet-dump or an arbitrary HTTP endpoint as EventPipe trace collection and suggesting a temporary SDK image can run dotnet-trace without installing it.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B better satisfies the core collection request by naming gc-verbose and providing the exact requested command. Its erroneous optional collect-linux recommendation is a meaningful flaw, and A has a better analysis workflow, but A misses the required profile and command entirely.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: HTTP 500s from downstream service on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: A substantially addresses the requested diagnosis with an applicable provider-based collection command and explains status and duration investigation. B is incomplete: it never supplies the trace collection command or providers needed to capture HTTP failures and timing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the requested diagnostic progression more coherently: collect a trace first, then escalate to a dump for suspected deadlock. A has stronger concrete dump commands and analysis details, but its sequencing and interpretation guidance are less aligned with diagnosing the type of hang.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: High CPU in Kubernetes on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: A satisfies every requested item, notably including an installation route for minimal container images. B has useful PID discovery and an explicit CPU-sampling profile, but omits the required installation guidance and its abbreviated sidecar configuration is not clearly sufficient to connect monitor to the application. The gap is meaningful but not large because both give a workable core collection and export workflow when the tool is present.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B answers with perfcollect and actionable setup/collection instructions tailored to pre-.NET 10 Linux, matching the central requested solution. A offers a potentially useful raw perf alternative, but misses the rubric's perfcollect recommendation and installation/use guidance; neither fully explains the dotnet-trace limitation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly addresses unattended automatic capture by coupling a circular buffer with a CPU-threshold stop condition. A largely requires someone to manually terminate the collection and therefore fails the central requirement, despite offering similar buffer options.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: B delivers the requested .NET Framework leak-collection workflow accurately and concretely: two well-timed full dumps, an allocation trace while growth occurs, and a clear explanation of dump diffing. A contains useful general suggestions, but its main dump timing is mismatched to a days-long leak, lacks the PerfView workflow, and includes a misleading restart heuristic.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the central, actionable leak-investigation collection plan: two time-separated dumps for comparison plus a trace during growth. A has useful telemetry ideas but omits the essential two-dump differential approach and includes a questionable suggestion to analyze a full dump with dotnet-gcdump.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly delivers the prescribed, actionable PerfView collection strategy and analysis targets. A contains some potentially useful general suggestions, but it misses the central provider/thread-time guidance and includes distracting or questionable configuration changes rather than focusing on collecting the needed data.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly fulfills the requested wait/block diagnostic approach with /ThreadTime, appropriate larger circular buffers, and a usable command. A's omission of /ThreadTime is a central technical failure, compounded by /OnlyManagedEvents, so its trace would not reliably provide the requested blocking analysis.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly satisfies every specified requirement with the correct host-based Windows-container tracing and symbol-handling workflow. A is plausible generic tracing advice but misses all rubric-specific elements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows modern .NET with admin high CPU
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly fulfills all three requested elements with a clear PerfView-first recommendation, a concise timed collection command, and actionable ETL analysis steps. A's dotnet-trace-first advice undermines its PerfView recommendation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Analyze healthy managed EXE activation
judgeRationales.rationale: No actual log content was included in the task, so both responses reasonably asked for the log. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline non-CLR-activation issue
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses handle the request essentially identically: they accept the flawed premise and ask for the CLR activation logs without recognizing that a NullReferenceException is a runtime error unrelated to CLR activation logging. Neither explains the actual scope of activation logs. Response B activated a domain skill but arrived at the same substantive answer without adding correct conceptual guidance. Quality of the final output is equivalent on all rubric criteria.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose FOD suppressed but activation still failing
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly ask for the logs before diagnosing, and neither delivers the full root-cause analysis. However, Response B activated the CLR activation debugging skill and correctly framed the problem in the right (legacy .NET Framework shim/COM activation) domain — mentioning v2 capping, SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS suppression, and COM activation paths that align with rubric items. Response A, by contrast, described modern .NET host (hostfxr/runtimeconfig.json) failure modes, which is the wrong codepath for CLR activation logs. B is more on-target but not dramatically better since both stopped short of the concrete fix.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose unexpected FOD dialog from native build tool
judgeRationales.rationale: Neither response had the actual logs to identify specific processes, but B activated the relevant CLR debugging skill and provided a substantively accurate diagnostic explanation of the FOD trigger mechanism (legacy capped bind, missing config, SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS control, suppressed-vs-launched). A merely asked for the logs with generic requests and provided no domain insight. B is much more useful and correct on the mechanism. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy in activation log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are similar in length and both miss the key technical points (CorBindToRuntimeEx equivalence, that the policy disables in-proc SxS, and the actual v4 decision in the log). However, B is more accurate: it correctly emphasizes running v2 components with CLR v4 in the same process and clarifies the policy does not force v2-first selection, whereas A's framing of loading 'CLR 2.0 side-by-side' is more misleading. B edges out A slightly.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain why same binary behaves differently under different launch methods
judgeRationales.rationale: B pinpoints the exact mechanism (SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS process error mode, inherited from parent, with same underlying capped bind failure) matching all rubric points. A gives a generic, hedged answer listing many possible context factors without identifying the real cause, and even implies incorrect divergence in downstream activation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify multiple activation sequences in a single log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly recognize they lack the actual log and request it rather than hallucinating an analysis. Neither addresses the substantive rubric criteria. However, Response B loaded the relevant clr-activation-debugging skill and referenced domain-accurate concepts (SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS, legacy capping, config presence, activation order) that align with the real diagnosis, demonstrating more relevant preparation. This gives B a slight edge.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, correct, and nearly equivalent: they recommend dotnet-trace with concrete commands and copy-out steps. A adds useful Kubernetes-specific tips (ephemeral debug container, restricted perf events) which are valuable, and avoids mentioning collect-linux entirely. B correctly conditions collect-linux on .NET 10+, so it satisfies the rubric, but introducing it adds slight risk. A is marginally better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly identifies perfcollect as the right tool for native stacks on .NET 8 Linux, correctly notes dotnet-trace misses native frames, and provides install/run guidance. A incorrectly leads with dotnet-trace and falsely claims it captures native frames, which is misleading for this scenario."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses miss PerfView's native /StopOnPerfCounter trigger, which would have been the ideal hands-off solution, and both correctly cover the circular buffer flags. A is slightly better because it provides a concrete, working watcher script including CPU normalization by core count and a named session for reliable stop, plus clearer emphasis on stopping during the spike. B's trigger approach is only described and even hints at timer-based capture that could catch recovery instead of the spike.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give solid, correct answers with procdump commands and PerfView traces. B aligns more precisely with the rubric: two dumps for diffing, explicit PerfView dump diff, and clear advice not to wait for OOM. A is broader and more thorough (PerfMon time-series, handle/native leak signals, PDBs) which is genuinely valuable, but it omits the key PerfView dump-diffing explanation and even suggests auto-dump on OOM, slightly against the 'capture during growth' guidance. B wins slightly on rubric alignment despite A's greater breadth."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns more closely with the intended rubric: it activated a skill, recommended dotnet-trace for allocation tracking while memory grows, explicitly ties the two-dump diff to identifying growing object types, and avoids raw dump commands and collect-linux. Response A is broader and technically excellent—arguably more comprehensive real-world advice with native vs managed leak separation and counters—but it misses the specific dotnet-trace allocation recommendation and gives direct dotnet-dump commands rather than a skill-based flow. B better matches the specific rubric expectations, so it wins slightly overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B aligns much more closely with the rubric's intended answer: PerfView with /ThreadTime and networking providers, listing all four providers, and explaining the combined value of thread-time + networking events. Response A offers a reasonable general diagnostic workflow (netsh trace, dotnet-trace, procdump, WinDbg) but doesn't center on the PerfView thread-time approach the rubric targets. Neither mentions RequestFailed events. B is clearly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses hit all rubric criteria. B's command syntax is cleaner and more correct (PerfView placement of /ThreadTime and collect, standard provider syntax), and it explicitly advises against a default stop trigger, aligning precisely with the rubric. A's command mixes some questionable/non-standard argument names (e.g., /KernelEvents:...NetTrace, /OnlyProviders with a raw keyword mask combined with named providers) that could fail to parse, adding risk. B is slightly better in correctness, though A is more thorough on providers.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly recommend PerfView from the host, but Response B hits all three rubric criteria: the critical /EnableEventsInContainers flag for process-isolation containers, the local-vs-merge analysis options, and merge /ImageIDsOnly for off-machine symbol resolution. Response A, while providing valid PerfView commands and useful PID discovery via crictl, misses all three of the container-specific technical details that make the trace actually usable in this scenario. Response B is substantially more correct for the specific environment described.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows modern .NET with admin high CPU
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B aligns precisely with all three rubric criteria: it recommends PerfView as the preferred tool for the Windows+admin scenario, gives a concrete PerfView collect command, and describes analyzing the .etl.zip in PerfView. Response A gives a reasonable but rubric-mismatched answer, defaulting to dotnet-trace and treating PerfView as secondary without a command. Both answers are technically valid, but B fulfills the intended requirements far better. Note that dotnet-trace is also a defensible technical choice, but per the rubric B is clearly favored.

judgeRationales.rationale: Both analyses find the central allocation problems and propose the right primary refactor. B is more precise and actionable, especially in correctly counting and locating the eight lowercasing sites and illustrating the append-based fix. Its extra minor findings are somewhat less important, but do not outweigh that stronger core analysis.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects Aggregate+Replace chain and struct missing IEquatable
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more comprehensive and better prioritizes the actual ToMetric dashboard hot path, while adding useful correctness caveats such as preserving culture behavior. Both cover the core required findings. B does include a few speculative or overstated micro-performance claims, while A incorrectly characterizes HasFlag as boxing; neither flaw overwhelms B's modest overall advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects CurrentCulture comparer and compiled regex budget in inflection rules
judgeRationales.rationale: A is the more reliable performance review for the stated workload: it actually benchmarks the concrete implementation, correctly weighs one-time startup cost against every-request matching throughput, and finds the important duplicate regex scan and culture/trim correctness defects. B provides useful counts and several valid observations, but its top-severity recommendation treats compiled regex as categorically bad despite the request-heavy scenario, and includes speculative or overstated claims (cache assumptions, Frozen collection speed, and List indexer overhead).

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers all core issues with more precise allocation accounting, source locations, implementation alternatives, prioritization, and semantic/framework caveats. A is concise and substantially correct, but its ValueStringBuilder sample is not directly usable as a public .NET API and its Pascalize allocation count is less complete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities
judgeRationales.rationale: A satisfies all requested performance findings while delivering and compiling concrete changes, plus a substantial differential-output check. B is a useful, more expansive review and surfaces additional possible concerns, but remains unvalidated and includes some overconfident or inaccurate allocation/severity assertions. The advantage is meaningful but not large because both cover the core review criteria well.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Investigate root cause of a .NET MAUI iOS crash
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly conclude that an unhandled managed startup exception was bridged to Objective-C and aborted, and both appropriately avoid claiming a missing managed message. A remains useful and offers a somewhat richer debugging checklist, so the gap is not large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Parse .NET frames and locate dSYMs from an iOS crash log

A supplies correct commands for both framework and runtime and better package guidance, though both omit the full libSystem.* image inventory.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reject Android tombstone passed as iOS crash log
judgeRationales.rationale: A provides the more careful technical result: it identifies the exact runtime/version and Build ID validation, gives source locations, and importantly flags the implausible handle_isinst frames as likely unwinder artifacts instead of presenting them as a genuine call chain. B is clearer about the Android-versus-Apple format/tool distinction, but uncritically reports those questionable frames as stack frames.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose FOD suppressed but activation still failing
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses satisfy all core diagnostic points and fixes. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose unexpected FOD dialog from native build tool

A's central conclusion—that the failure is harmless and the log shows only success—undermines its diagnosis and troubleshooting advice.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Investigate root cause of a .NET MAUI iOS crash
judgeRationales.rationale: Both reached the same correct core diagnosis: an unhandled managed exception during MAUI startup promoted to a SIGABRT, with the managed exception message missing from the .ips. B did deeper and more verifiable work: it used the symbolication skill, parsed the crash properly, surfaced the 'abort() called' ASI message, and genuinely resolved the CoreCLR startup path (RunMain → ExecuteMainMethod → coreclr_execute_assembly) by downloading the matching CoreCLR dSYM by UUID. A produced a solid, accurate answer with correct address calculations but did not resolve the CoreCLR frames or surface the ASI. Neither fully satisfied criterion 4 (SDK pack/NuGet cache paths). B's more thorough and grounded analysis makes it slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Parse .NET frames and locate dSYMs from an iOS crash log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly parsed the two-part .ips format and generated structurally correct atos commands. However, B went substantially further: it activated the symbolication skill, actually located and downloaded the correct libcoreclr dSYM from the Microsoft symbol server via the UUID-addressed path, verified the embedded UUID matched the crash, and validated that the atos offsets resolve to real symbols (CallDescrWorkerInternal, RunMain, etc.). A stopped at claiming 'dSYMs are not available in this workspace' and provided only expected/hypothetical paths without actually locating them. Neither named the exact NuGet runtime package, but B's concrete verification and symbol-server discovery make it meaningfully more complete and correct on the core task of locating the dSYM."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Reject Android tombstone passed as iOS crash log
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly identified the Android tombstone format and the intentional abort. However, B went far beyond A: it downloaded the exact matching Mono debug symbols from the Microsoft symbol server using the Build ID, then ran addr2line to produce accurate source-level symbolication (function names and file:line), revealing the true root cause (Environment.FailFast('not compatible')). A only provided instructions and speculated about the abort message without actually resolving the frames — and its frame descriptions were guesses that turned out less accurate than B's verified results. B delivered the actual symbolicated stack, which is what the task asked for, making it substantially better on final output quality.

However, B stopped at asking for information without probing the environment for dump files or analysis tools, better aligning with 'does not attempt to open or analyze.' A actively searched for dumps and checked for lldb/gdb/dotnet-dump, edging closer to the disallowed behavior. Thus B is slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect runtime and configure crash dumps for unknown .NET app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: B is technically more correct: it recognizes PID 12345 resolves to Node.js in the environment and warns the user, uses stronger runtime detection (Rhp symbol for NativeAOT plus a proper 'undetermined' fallback), and—most importantly—provides the correct NativeAOT configuration using OS core dumps rather than incorrectly reusing the CoreCLR DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump env vars as A does. A's NativeAOT config is factually wrong. This makes B clearly better overall despite A being slightly cleaner on avoiding dump analysis. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recover crash dump from macOS NativeAOT without createdump
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are correct and useful. B directly addresses the key rubric points: checking /cores explicitly and clearly explaining that the core dump is lost if ulimit wasn't set beforehand. A provides more context (Console.app, dSYM symbolication) but frames ulimit only as future guidance rather than explaining the current dump may be gone. B is slightly better aligned with the rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up NativeAOT crash dumps with createdump in Kubernetes
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B correctly uses the full executable path for DOTNET_DbgCreateDumpToolPath (matching .NET 11 docs) and properly adds SYS_PTRACE in the securityContext. Response A introduces a critical error by insisting the tool path must be a directory, which would break dump collection, and omits SYS_PTRACE from the actual spec. Response B verified its answer against reference material, while Response A hallucinated the directory requirement."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Investigate runtime upgrade performance impact
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully set up and ran BenchmarkDotNet comparisons across .NET 9 and .NET 10 with good practices. The decisive difference is correctness of conclusions: the expected outcome is two methods ~2-3x faster and UniqueWordCount unchanged. B nailed this, explicitly recognizing host-load noise, repeating runs, and correctly reporting UniqueWordCount as inconclusive/no reliable difference. A ran under very high load, reported inflated and likely wrong deltas (including a bogus 43% speedup for UniqueWordCount), and though it caveated the numbers, its final table presents misleading conclusions. B's methodical handling of noise and accurate final verdict make it clearly better overall. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Catches compound allocations in recursive number converter with ToLower
judgeRationales.rationale: Both fail to deliver the requested performance analysis because no source was available. A's final response is marginally more useful: it clearly asks for the missing code and provides practical ways to supply it, while B focuses on unavailable reference files and only then requests source.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects Aggregate+Replace chain and struct missing IEquatable
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers the shared core findings while adding useful parsing-path allocation findings, HasFlag overhead, and an explicit positive assessment of existing FrozenDictionary usage. Its proposed one-match replacement has potential semantic limitations, so the overall advantage is modest rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects CurrentCulture comparer and compiled regex budget in inflection rules
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more evidence-based and complete, with exact counts, locations, caveats, and a useful observation about immutable irregular dictionaries. A usefully suggests result caching, but omits cache invalidation concerns if rules can be added after use and includes a weak reverse-loop micro-optimization. Both have broadly similar core findings.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more complete and prioritized, notably recognizing the existing GeneratedRegex positive practice and identifying the apparent redundant compiled regex fields. A is cleaner and more precise on Pascalize allocation counting, while B includes a somewhat incomplete illustrative Underscore implementation and an understated Pascalize count, so the overall advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more complete on the principal string-allocation issue by covering Hungarian as well as Swedish, while retaining all required findings and the important mutable-cache exception. A's unsupported memoization suggestion is less reliably beneficial in a tight-loop library context due to cache growth and synchronization considerations.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: A performs a substantive, prioritized performance review with concrete findings and fixes, including the key format-string allocation issues. Although it omits the requested positive observation and contains somewhat rough size estimates, it is vastly more useful than B, which merely asks for code despite the code being available to the agent.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: Both cover all core performance issues accurately. B is more complete and concrete, explicitly documenting positive existing choices and providing better-grounded implementation sketches. Its extra low-value findings and verbosity do not materially outweigh that advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds per-call Dictionary allocation not hoisted to static
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy all core findings with actionable fixes. B is modestly stronger overall because it additionally calls out the repeated hot-path Math.Pow calls, gives locations and a concrete loop refactor. Its unsealed-class suggestion is speculative and some count details are noisy, so this is only a slight advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds repeated enumeration in time and collection formatting
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Flags Span inconsistencies and compound method chains in truncation library
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly satisfies all three rubric items and gives concrete locations and span-specific guidance. A adds a useful observation about the character truncator's two passes and has sensible lookup alternatives, but it misses the requested explicit span-consistency comparison.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identifies unsealed leaf classes and locale hierarchy patterns
judgeRationales.rationale: B gives the requested hierarchy-focused review with accurate, concrete findings and an important positive registry observation. A has useful points, but its method-hiding recommendation is technically unsound and several additional recommendations are speculative or weakly justified.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Symbolicate multi-thread tombstone

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Catches compound allocations in recursive number converter with ToLower
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, cover all rubric points, correctly count the 8 ToLower sites, identify the compound allocation issue, recommend StringBuilder/ToLowerInvariant, and flag the long.MinValue overflow bug. B is slightly better: it provides more precise line-level evidence tying the += and interpolation paths together, a structured checklist confirming absence of other anti-patterns, the sealed-class devirtualization insight, and an appropriate disclaimer. A is more concise and equally correct on the core findings, but B's analysis is marginally more thorough and evidence-backed. The difference is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects Aggregate+Replace chain and struct missing IEquatable
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core bottlenecks (transcendental math, linear prefix scan, Aggregate/Replace allocations, string formatting, HasFlag). B additionally addresses the IEquatable struct concern and correctly recognizes FrozenDictionary as a positive finding, matching two rubric criteria that A misses (A actively argues against FrozenDictionary). A slightly edges out on the char.ToString() specificity. Neither suggests the .Contains() short-circuit. On balance B satisfies more rubric criteria and is more thorough and structured, giving it a slight overall advantage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects CurrentCulture comparer and compiled regex budget in inflection rules
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, methodical, and identify the same core issues: linear regex scan on every miss, double regex scan (IsMatch+Replace), culture-sensitive uncountable lookup, compiled regex startup cost, and mutable-collection/freeze concerns. A is more concise and adds a clear priority ordering and precedence-preservation note. B verified rule counts empirically (46 = 19+27, matching the actual code) whereas A's 44 count is slightly inaccurate, and B better matches rubric framing (ASCII English hot path, per-instance recompilation, source-generated regex). B's extensive empirical grep-based scanning gives it a slight edge in correctness and coverage. Both are high quality with no errors; B is marginally more accurate and rubric-aligned.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core hot-path issues (Underscore replace chain, Pascalize per-match allocation, Camelize re-work). Response A adds valuable correctness observations (culture-sensitivity, Pascalize regex bug) that show deeper reasoning. However, Response B covers more rubric criteria: it recognizes the [GeneratedRegex] positive finding, addresses the compiled-regex budget with explicit counts, and flags the InflectionRule dynamic compiled regex — three criteria A misses entirely. B is more comprehensive and structured, making it slightly better overall despite A's stronger correctness commentary.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses cover all 5 rubric criteria correctly, catching long.MinValue recursion, concatenation, List allocation, string comparison, and correctly avoiding the FrozenDictionary trap on the mutable cache. B is slightly better: it more directly and cleanly recommends FrozenDictionary for the immutable dicts (rubric item 2), explicitly notes the mutable cache should NOT be Frozen as a positive pattern (item 5), and provides a more structured, verifiable analysis (line-counted checklist). A adds a valuable concurrency finding (Dictionary cache unsafe for parallel access) which is a genuine plus, but slightly muddies the FrozenDictionary recommendation by leaning toward arrays. Overall roughly comparable with a small edge to B.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: The task was to 'review for performance.' B delivered a well-structured, prioritized performance review with concrete findings, correct counts, severity ratings, positive findings, and a benchmark-caveat disclaimer—directly addressing three of four rubric criteria. A instead pursued a risky series of perl/apply_patch edits to modify the file (which was arguably not asked), and its final output is a terse implementation summary that only loosely covers the rubric points and does not surface a review with the positive IEquatable finding. While A verified compilation, it did not confirm behavioral correctness of aggressive edits, and its deliverable is weaker as a performance review. B is clearly better across most criteria. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core hot-path allocation issues (LINQ pipeline, per-match ToLower, params array, recursive reprocessing) without modifying the fixture. B is more precise with line references, explicitly identifies the Dehumanize string.Concat(words.Select) pattern, and importantly captures the span-based Concat helpers as a positive finding, which A omits entirely. B did struggle with tooling (rg not found) but recovered via grep. A is more concise and adds useful CMS-level caching/culture recommendations, but misses two rubric points B hits. judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET 10 on Linux with root access and native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: The task's rubric centers on recommending dotnet-trace collect-linux, the modern .NET 10 preferred approach. Response B correctly identifies and provides this tool with a concrete command, satisfying most criteria. Response A gives a reasonable, technically valid perf-based answer but entirely misses the intended collect-linux recommendation, failing the core criteria.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET Framework on Windows without admin privileges
judgeRationales.rationale: B better matches the rubric's focus: it explicitly names PerfView as the primary .NET Framework CPU tool requiring admin, clearly states there is no non-admin trace fallback, and directs the user to obtain admin. A is broader and more practically useful (PerfMon counters, logs, dumps) but misses the key rubric point of naming PerfView and the trace-fallback gap. Since grading is rubric-aligned, B wins slightly. A's breadth is valuable but less targeted to the specific rubric criteria.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assembly loading failure on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses give reasonable, valid approaches to getting dotnet-trace into a container without the SDK, and both correctly note only the runtime is needed. Neither hits the ideal rubric answers (aka.ms direct binary links, curl download of the tool itself, kubectl cp). A provides an actual curl-based download flow that works self-contained inside the container, which is closer to the rubric's curl/download intent and is robust. B relies on a host-side dotnet install and docker cp — practical but assumes a host with dotnet SDK, somewhat contradicting the SDK-free premise, and uses docker cp rather than kubectl cp. A is slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B nails the key rubric requirement of --profile gc-verbose, which A misses by recommending gc-collect and a raw provider string instead. Both correctly avoid recommending collect-linux for .NET 8 — B mentions it but properly gates it to .NET 10+, while A omits it entirely (a slight edge for A on that single criterion). B also adds useful handoff metadata. Since gc-verbose is the central technical requirement and appears twice in the rubric, B wins overall, though not by a huge margin since both are largely correct and helpful.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: HTTP 500s from downstream service on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly recommends dotnet-trace with System.Net.Http providers, explains RequestStop status codes for identifying 5xx, covers timing, and gives the exact command — matching the task intent. A recommends tcpdump, which cannot see status codes on encrypted TLS traffic and misses the core answer. B's only flaw is mentioning collect-linux gated on .NET 10+, a minor issue that doesn't outweigh its clear superiority.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns more closely with the intended diagnostic workflow: start with a trace, escalate to a dump for true deadlocks if the trace is inconclusive, and analyze with lldb+SOS. It also distinguishes livelock/starvation/deadlock. Response A is more comprehensive and practically detailed (counters, gdb, mitigations, dependency checks) and would be genuinely useful, but it doesn't structure the trace-then-conditional-dump escalation the rubric emphasizes and omits lldb/SOS and livelock terminology. B wins on all five rubric points, though A's broader practical depth keeps the gap modest rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: High CPU in Kubernetes on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B better matches the intended answer: it leads with dotnet-trace inside the pod, positions dotnet-monitor as the no-shell-access alternative, and includes kubectl cp for extracting the trace. A inverts the priority (dotnet-monitor first) and omits how to get the trace out of the container. A does offer more breadth (gcdump, dumps, stacks), but on the specific rubric criteria B is clearly stronger.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers correctly recommend dotnet-trace with the collect command and neither wrongly suggests collect-linux. B is more thorough: it explicitly addresses the .NET 8 / collect-linux caveat, includes install/PATH steps, PID discovery via dotnet-trace ps, and native-stack guidance via perfcollect. A is solid and slightly cleaner (speedscope format), but B provides more accurate, complete guidance aligned with all rubric points.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: Neither response uses the ideal perfcollect tool the rubric expects. However, A correctly centers the answer on perf (the right tool for native stacks) and correctly notes dotnet-trace is for managed analysis, while B leads with dotnet-trace and inaccurately claims it captures native frames, only recommending perf as a fallback. A's technical accuracy on the core question (native frames need perf, not dotnet-trace) makes it slightly better.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are similar in quality: correct circular buffer args, similar explanations, and neither uses PerfView's native /StopOnPerfCounter trigger (the ideal answer). B is slightly better because it provides a concrete, unattended automation mechanism (a working PowerShell watcher with core-count normalization and consecutive-sample confirmation) that directly addresses the user's 'can't sit and watch it' constraint, plus more practical tuning notes and an offer for Task Scheduler XML. A's trigger path is vaguer.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, near-equivalent, and correct across most criteria. Neither invokes a dump-collect skill. A is marginally better because it more explicitly describes diffing dumps to identify which object types are growing (comparing object type growth and GC roots). B is also excellent with good filename/timestamp synchronization advice, but slightly less explicit on the object-diffing explanation. The gap is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B matches all four rubric criteria closely: PerfView with /ThreadTime, the full set of networking providers, the thread-time + networking events explanation, and RequestFailed events. Response A gives a reasonable and technically sound answer (dotnet-trace + netsh) but does not align with the specific expected approach and misses RequestFailed and the thread-time blocking framing. B is clearly better on the rubric while remaining accurate."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly recommend PerfView /ThreadTime with large buffers, no stop trigger, and a concrete command line. A provides richer explanation of how ThreadTime/context-switch data reveals waits and blocking, and guidance on analysis views. B adds useful ASP.NET Core/Kestrel and networking providers, which is a nice touch, but A's syntax is slightly more accurate on the kernel context-switch specifics and its explanation is stronger. Overall a slight edge to A.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B satisfies all three rubric criteria: it uses /EnableEventsInContainers, explains preserving symbols by merging before the container exits, and mentions merge /ImageIDsOnly. Response A, while a reasonable general answer, misses all three specific expectations — it targets a host PID without container event enablement (less reliable for Windows containers), doesn't address the ephemeral container shutdown/symbol merge problem, and omits /ImageIDsOnly. B is substantially more correct and complete for this specific scenario."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows modern .NET with admin high CPU
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B directly satisfies all three rubric criteria: it recommends PerfView as the preferred tool, provides a specific PerfView collect command, and describes analyzing the resulting .etl.zip in the CPU Stacks view. Response A instead centers on dotnet-trace and mentions PerfView only as a viewer, missing the core of every criterion. While Response A is a reasonable answer in general, it does not align with what the rubric rewards, making B clearly superior for this task."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: CoreCLR Alpine Docker non-root configuration
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are solid and advisory. B is superior because it covers the critical SYS_PTRACE capability and seccomp requirements needed for createdump in containers, uses the current DOTNET_ env var prefix, and adds Kubernetes and diagnostics considerations. A misses SYS_PTRACE and uses legacy COMPlus_ naming. The gap is meaningful but not enormous since A's core advice is otherwise correct.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: NativeAOT Kubernetes dump collection setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are structurally similar and share the same shortcomings (wrong env var name for tool path, wrong dump type for NativeAOT). B is better because it correctly adds the SYS_PTRACE capability, which is important for dump tooling in containers and which A omits entirely. This gives B an edge on one distinct rubric criterion while tying on the rest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: macOS NativeAOT crash dump recovery steps
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are similar and correct, but A covers the /cores directory and includes ulimit -c unlimited, satisfying two rubric criteria that B misses. A is also slightly more complete (symbols, image list). Both avoid execution and premature analysis equally.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure CoreCLR dump collection in Alpine Docker as non-root
judgeRationales.rationale: The SYS_PTRACE capability is a critical requirement (explicitly a rubric item) that A includes and B entirely omits — without it, crash dump generation frequently fails in containers. B has advantages (modern DOTNET_ prefix, host-side permissions handling, cleanup note), but the missing SYS_PTRACE is the most functionally important gap. On balance A is slightly better overall because it satisfies the harder correctness requirement, though B is stronger on modernity and permissions detail.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure automatic crash dumps for CoreCLR app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are essentially equivalent: correct env vars, directory setup, systemd guidance, verification steps, and neither over-reaches into dump analysis. Content quality is the same across all criteria.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline dump analysis request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses avoided opening the dump or installing tools. However, the key rubric criterion is clearly stating the analysis is out of scope. Response B does this explicitly ('I can't directly analyze .dmp files here'), while Response A implies it will perform the analysis itself. Although B mentions tools like dotnet-dump, lldb, and windbg (borderline against the spirit of criterion 3), it only guides the user rather than executing anything. B better satisfies the primary scope criterion, making it slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect runtime and configure crash dumps for unknown .NET app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong and satisfy nearly all criteria: they detect the runtime first, use inspection to distinguish CoreCLR vs NativeAOT, provide runtime-appropriate config, avoid assumptions, and don't analyze dumps. Response A is slightly more thorough and reliable — it uses /proc/maps loaded-library detection (robust for a running process), adds the dotnet-dump ps cross-check, and covers both system core dumps (systemd-coredump, LimitCORE) and the DOTNET_Dbg env vars while clarifying which applies to CoreCLR. Response B is clean and correct but slightly less complete, and its strings-for-CorExeMain check is a weaker signal. The gap is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recover crash dump from macOS NativeAOT without createdump
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses provide essentially identical guidance: DiagnosticReports folders and Console.app. Both miss the /cores/ directory and the ulimit -c point. Both correctly avoid analyzing dump contents. B adds slightly more context about what the report contains and re-reproducing, but neither is meaningfully better on the rubric criteria. Effectively equal.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up NativeAOT crash dumps with createdump in Kubernetes
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are broadly similar and both miss the correct env var names (DOTNET_DbgCreateDumpToolPath) and the correct dump type (4). However, A includes the critical SYS_PTRACE capability required for createdump to work, which B omits entirely. A also uses the modern DOTNET_ prefix rather than B's legacy COMPlus_ prefix, making it more appropriate for .NET 11. Ironically B loaded a dedicated skill but produced a weaker answer. A is slightly better overall, primarily due to the SYS_PTRACE inclusion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Catches compound allocations in recursive number converter with ToLower
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the core issues: the long.MinValue overflow bug, 8 redundant .ToLower() sites, and string concatenation allocations, and both recommend StringBuilder/Span and deferred lowercasing. B is more precise and thorough: it maps specific line numbers to concrete allocation counts, explicitly recommends ToLowerInvariant, and provides a well-structured prioritized report with severity ratings. A is solid and clean but slightly less explicit on the compound-allocation breakdown and correctness naming. A had a minor garbled character ('短-lived'). The difference is modest since both cover the substantive findings.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects Aggregate+Replace chain and struct missing IEquatable
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects CurrentCulture comparer and compiled regex budget in inflection rules
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly cover all four rubric criteria and are of high, accurate quality. A is slightly more explicit on the ASCII-English rationale. However, B is more thorough and rigorous: it uses the domain skill, performs a systematic verification scan with counts, clearly ranks findings by severity, identifies the unsealed leaf class devirtualization opportunity, adds positive findings, and cross-references line numbers verified against the source. A also includes a couple of valid extra points (regex timeout, CultureInvariant), but B's structured, verified, prioritized presentation and methodical approach make it marginally stronger overall. Both avoided errors and neither got stuck.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detects compiled regex startup budget and regex chain allocations
judgeRationales.rationale: The task was to analyze the library for performance issues. Response B delivered a thorough, well-structured analysis covering nearly all rubric points: the compiled regex budget, triple-replace chain, culture-sensitive casing, per-match Pascalize allocation, GeneratedRegex as a positive, and InflectionRule compiled-regex remediation. Response A chose to rewrite the code, which is a valid but riskier approach; its output summary covers fewer of the specific analysis points, does not credit GeneratedRegex, omits the InflectionRule issue, and doesn't surface the compiled-regex budget. Both compiled/verified where relevant (A compiled successfully), but on the actual analytical rubric B is clearly stronger across the board. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds StringComparison.Ordinal missing and FrozenDictionary opportunities
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more precise on line numbers and formatting, giving it edges on criteria 1 and 2. However, criterion 5 is the key differentiator: A correctly recognizes _runtimeCache as a mutable, unbounded, thread-unsafe cache — a substantive and correct hot-path finding — while B omits it entirely, missing a genuine issue. Both cover the core findings (string +=, List capacity, Ordinal). A's correct handling of the trickier mutated-cache distinction tips the balance slightly to A overall despite B's superior presentation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: The task was a performance review. B delivers a thorough, structured review that hits 3 of 4 rubric points explicitly (cascading Replace, StringBuilder/handler suggestion, IEquatable positive finding) with precise file:line references and prioritized severity. A actually applied code changes and verified they compile, which is valuable, but its final output is a terse summary that omits the IEquatable positive finding, doesn't suggest StringBuilder/string.Create, and articulates findings less clearly as a review. A's edits were done via fragile python string-replacement with verification, showing methodical recovery from tool failures. Both are competent, but B better satisfies the review-oriented rubric. Slightly better rather than much, since A did produce a validated working improvement.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, correct, and avoid modifying the fixture. They tie on most criteria (Cast/Select pipeline, ToLower allocation, params overload). B edges ahead by more precisely identifying the All(char.IsUpper) enumeration and the Dehumanize Select allocation, and notably by recognizing the existing span-based Concat helpers as a positive finding, which A entirely omits. A is well-organized and concise, but B covers more rubric points accurately.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds per-call Dictionary allocation not hoisted to static
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly cover all five rubric criteria. The task asked to 'review for performance issues' — B delivers a precise, well-organized review with exact line numbers, severity ratings, quantified allocation analysis, and concrete fixes, directly matching the deliverable. It also verified findings via scans. A instead applied the fixes and validated by compiling/running, which is valuable, but its summary is terser and less explanatory of the individual issues; the task requested a review rather than a rewrite. A did verify correctness by building and running the output, which is a genuine strength. B's diagnostic depth and clearer articulation of the allocation chain give it a slight edge for the review task, though the gap is small since both are correct and thorough."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds repeated enumeration in time and collection formatting
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong and cover nearly all rubric criteria with correct line references and actionable fixes. The key differentiator is criterion 4: B explicitly identifies the Enumerable.Reverse static-initialization allocation and correctly frames it as a one-time cost, while A omits it entirely. B also adds quantified scan counts and severity ratings while appropriately distinguishing per-call from one-time and API-breaking concerns. A is more concise and equally accurate on the shared points, but B's fuller coverage gives it a slight edge overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Flags Span inconsistencies and compound method chains in truncation library
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly identify the main hot-path issues: word truncator allocations, TrimEnd double allocation, double scanning, and symbol lookup lists. B is more thorough and methodical, providing a scan checklist, exact counts, severity table, and slightly more precise treatment of the List<char>[] heap-allocation issue (matching the ReadOnlySpan rubric point). B also appropriately cautions about semantic correctness before changing scan logic. A is more concise and accurate but slightly less precise on the symbol-lookup criterion. Neither explicitly frames the Span-usage inconsistency. Overall B is slightly better due to greater rigor and closer alignment with criterion 3.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identifies unsealed leaf classes and locale hierarchy patterns
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly cover the core sealing findings and the DefaultOrdinalizer base-class nuance. Neither captures the OrdinalIgnoreCase positive finding well; B mentions it but mischaracterizes it and adds a dubious thread-safety claim. B provides more complete enumeration of leaf classes and a thorough scan checklist, and both correctly flag the ToString/ToLowerInvariant allocation. A is more concise and its extra caveat about JIT devirtualization nuance is sound. On balance B's greater completeness edges it slightly ahead, though its incorrect thread-safety assertion is a minor demerit.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are solid, methodical diagnostic guides that emphasize capturing evidence before restarting. However, Response B aligns much more closely with every rubric criterion: it leads with a thread-time trace, distinguishes livelocks/starvation/deadlocks explicitly, conditions the dump on the trace being insufficient, and names lldb+SOS. Response A is competent but relies on dumps and dotnet-stack, missing the lldb/SOS detail and the livelock distinction, and does not frame the dump as a trace-dependent follow-up. Response B also correctly leveraged the dotnet-trace skill despite some file-view errors it recovered from.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: High CPU in Kubernetes on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are high quality, accurate, and satisfy all five rubric criteria without recommending the .NET 10+ collect-linux command. B aligns more tightly with the rubric's intent: it leads with dotnet-trace as the preferred approach, explicitly positions dotnet-monitor as the alternative when console access is unavailable with a concrete REST example, and warns about provider override behavior. A is also excellent and arguably more comprehensive (counters, dumps, K8s considerations), but its dotnet-monitor framing is only for 'ongoing production' rather than the no-console fallback. The gap is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: Both correctly identify that dotnet-trace only captures managed stacks and both provide valid technical guidance. However, the rubric specifically expects perfcollect, which B recommends with complete install/collect/view instructions, verified against actual documentation and script options. A instead uses raw perf record — a technically valid alternative but not the expected answer, and it misses several rubric points. B is much better aligned with the rubric.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are high quality and technically sound, correctly recommending PerfView with /StopOnPerfCounter and a circular buffer. B is slightly better overall because it satisfies the rubric more completely: it includes both /CircularMB and /BufferSizeMB, and it explicitly explains the crucial point that the trigger must fire on the spike rather than the recovery to avoid the buffer overwriting the event. A's added Task Scheduler guidance and MinSecForTrigger detail are useful but do not offset the missed 'not the recovery' explanation and the omitted /BufferSizeMB. A also verified its args against PerfView source, but the final answer still lacked those two elements the rubric weights.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B aligns much more closely with the rubric: it provides concrete procdump and PerfView commands, explicitly frames two dumps for diffing, describes PerfView heap diff analysis to identify growing objects, and clearly advises against waiting for the OOM. Response A is a solid, thorough general answer with good counter guidance but lacks concrete commands, PerfView allocation tracing, and the dump-diff analysis explanation that the rubric emphasizes. Both are technically sound; B better matches the specific desired guidance."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong, correct, and cover the essential diagnostic data: two dumps for diffing, allocation traces during growth, environment details, counters, and native memory investigation. They tie on most rubric criteria. B edges ahead by referencing the repository's dump-collect procedure rather than providing direct dump commands, matching the intended skill-based approach, and by handling the tooling more precisely with proper duration flags. A is arguably more comprehensive with richer application-correlation guidance and a clearer diagnostic decision tree, but includes minor inaccuracies (e.g., 'pooh-size' typo, direct dump commands). The differences are small, so B is only slightly better overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)

Response A gives a broader, still-correct layered approach (dotnet-trace, netsh trace, pktmon) but does not center on the specific PerfView /ThreadTime + Providers technique the rubric rewards. B is more targeted and better matches all criteria despite A being competent and comprehensive.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows modern .NET with admin high CPU

B also recovered gracefully from view tool failures using bash. B is much better against this rubric."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: NativeAOT Kubernetes dump collection setup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses hit nearly all rubric criteria: SYS_PTRACE, volume mount, dump type 4, and advisory-only guidance. The decisive difference is the DOTNET_DbgCreateDumpToolPath value. Response A confidently asserts the variable takes the directory (/opt/tools), which is factually incorrect—the runtime expects the full path to the createdump executable. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Advisory: macOS NativeAOT crash dump recovery steps

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure CoreCLR dump collection in Alpine Docker as non-root

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Configure automatic crash dumps for CoreCLR app on Linux

Response A is slightly better: it notes the critical systemd %% escaping requirement (without which the DbgMiniDumpName variable is malformed in a unit file — B omits this), adds a controlled SIGABRT test to actually validate dump generation, includes journalctl/file verification, and mentions the legacy COMPlus_ prefix and security considerations. Response B is cleaner and more concise but misses the systemd escaping caveat.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline dump analysis request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are essentially equivalent. Neither correctly identified that dump analysis is out of scope for this skill (the workspace contained a 'dump-collect' skill focused on collecting dumps, not analyzing them). Both instead offered to perform the analysis once the dump was provided. Neither attempted to open a dump or install analysis tools, so those criteria are satisfied by both. Response B did marginally more discovery by finding the SKILL.md files, but it still failed to leverage that information to state the scope limitation, so the outcome is the same. Overall a tie."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Detect runtime and configure crash dumps for unknown .NET app on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly detect the runtime before configuring, use valid inspection techniques, cover both runtimes conditionally, and avoid dump analysis. Response A is slightly more complete and practically actionable: it offers concrete systemd unit configuration for both runtimes, correctly notes that env vars require a process restart (adding an on-demand dotnet-dump path for the running PID), and gives clearer inspection/export steps. Response B correctly notes PID 12345 isn't present and gives solid guidance but is marginally less coherent in mixing ulimit/core_pattern with systemd. The gap is small.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Set up NativeAOT crash dumps with createdump in Kubernetes

B also used the provided skill/reference material methodically, while A relied on web fetches and produced two substantive errors. Both tie on volume mounting, dump type, and not analyzing dumps."

judgeRationales.rationale: Both find the principal hot-path allocation and culture issues. B is more complete and grounded, including Camelize's extra copy and InflectionRule.Apply's double match, and avoids A's materially incorrect GeneratedRegex recommendation for dynamic InflectionRule patterns. Some ancillary claims are debatable, but B is the stronger final analysis overall.

judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy every core finding. B is slightly more audit-friendly through exact counts, locations, explicit .NET-version caveat, and clearer prioritization. judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation
judgeRationales.rationale: B covers the key formatting allocations while adding useful, well-prioritized findings about the oversized eagerly computed struct, value-copy cost, and lossy Bits-based equality/comparison. A is strong on the specific Replace branches but overstates the unit-order issue and is less comprehensive.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy every required finding well. A is slightly more focused and better prioritized for the stated hot path, while also catching the final range/concatenation allocation and Split/join issue. B is systematic and useful, but adds a comparatively speculative/low-value sealing recommendation, has an inconsistent claim that all findings are maximally severe while labeling them moderate, and includes unnecessary boilerplate disclaimer.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds per-call Dictionary allocation not hoisted to static
judgeRationales.rationale: The substantive review findings are essentially identical, and A provides a more directly inspectable sample refactor. However, B reports actually applying the changes and gives credible compile/run verification with representative output, making its claimed final result slightly stronger overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds repeated enumeration in time and collection formatting
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy every requested finding and give useful hot-path allocation guidance. A is more focused and concrete on the target code paths, especially the object formatter, and avoids B's blanket severity framing and less-certain unsealed-class recommendation.

Its unsupported speed multipliers and questionable suggestion to replace arbitrary number.ToString() fallbacks temper the advantage, so the overall lead is slight.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Analyze healthy managed EXE activation
judgeRationales.rationale: B fully answers the request with a grounded, correct explanation of the successful CLR activation. A merely asks the user to supply a log even though the evaluation environment supplied one, so it fails the task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Decline non-CLR-activation issue
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses correctly reject the premise and give useful next steps. B is slightly stronger overall because its explanation of the specific activation-log scope is more technically precise, while A's empty-directory check and additional artifact suggestions are also useful.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose FOD suppressed but activation still failing
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more technically precise and directly grounded in the trace: it identifies the debug-symbol COM class activation, explains the capped COM path, and separates the actual failed bind from the FOD re-check. A reaches the broadly correct remediation but includes a misleading claim that mt.exe itself is a legacy managed/mixed-mode executable and adds less reliable speculation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Diagnose unexpected FOD dialog from native build tool
judgeRationales.rationale: Both outputs reach the core correct diagnosis. B is more technically precise about the COM components, capped legacy policy, and the difference between suppression and recovery. A also includes a questionable broad registry workaround and presents installing NetFx3 as an equally preferred quick fix, whereas B better prioritizes correcting mt.exe's activation configuration.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy in activation log
judgeRationales.rationale: B is substantively aligned with the CLR activation behavior and covers the key SxS trade-off. A gets the core semantic effect backwards, so its otherwise clear presentation would mislead the user about runtime selection.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Explain why same binary behaves differently under different launch methods
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are correct and directly answer the question. B is modestly stronger because it more fully explains the capped legacy-binding context and offers a plausible configuration-based remediation in addition to NetFx3 installation, while preserving the key conclusion that error mode only suppresses the dialog.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Identify multiple activation sequences in a single log
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the central causal diagnosis for intermittent behavior—legacy binding order and reuse of the global legacy runtime—and recommends the appropriate policy/configuration fix. A gets the two paths and capping evidence right but incorrectly reduces the problem to NetFx3 presence across machines and recommends installing v2.0 as the primary fix.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET 10 on Linux with root access and native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the tailored .NET 10/kernel 6.8/root use case with the intended tool, a usable command, and the relevant native/kernel tracing rationale. A offers potentially useful older perf-based alternatives, but misses the preferred collect-linux workflow and makes an overly broad claim about dotnet-trace.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: .NET Framework on Windows without admin privileges
judgeRationales.rationale: B aligns closely with every required limitation and recommendation: no non-admin CPU trace path for .NET Framework, no dotnet-trace, limited dump value, and obtain admin/ask an admin for PerfView. A is more expansive but materially misleads on the viability of non-admin ETW and dumps for finding CPU hot paths.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Assembly loading failure on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B is more focused on the startup-crash scenario and provides a clean, directly usable launch command. A is also substantively correct and adds useful LoaderExceptions and ALC event diagnostics, but its opening contains distracting, explicitly incorrect false starts and an unnecessary host-trace diversion.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Container installation without .NET SDK
judgeRationales.rationale: B is the clearer, more directly executable answer: it supplies an end-to-end kubectl/docker collection workflow, includes a bounded collection duration, and covers the no-console sidecar case. A is also strong, but its first 'single-file' option misleadingly suggests a normal dotnet tool install output can simply be copied as a standalone binary; its direct-download option is the reliable one. B has a minor overbroad 'No root required' statement, but this does not outweigh its overall practical clarity.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Excessive GC on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers satisfy the core request accurately. B is slightly stronger because it directly explains why a trace rather than a dump is needed and stays tightly focused on the requested collection workflow. A is more expansive and useful in places, but its extra dump/configuration guidance is not necessary to answer the trace-collection question.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: HTTP 500s from downstream service on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Hang or deadlock diagnosis on Linux
judgeRationales.rationale: B better follows the requested diagnostic progression: trace first to classify the hang, then dump/debugger escalation for deadlock, while clearly distinguishing the relevant failure modes. A is a strong and more operationally detailed playbook, especially for dump analysis, but misses the trace-first and livelock-focused framing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: High CPU in Kubernetes on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers are substantially correct and actionable. B is especially concise and robust about obtaining the tool without an SDK, but A covers the full diagnostic progression (counters, CPU trace, optional dump), Kubernetes considerations, and the important dotnet-monitor alternative, making it more complete for the stated production scenario.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Kubernetes with console access prefers console tools
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: tie). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Linux pre-.NET 10 needing native call stacks
judgeRationales.rationale: Both answers satisfy the core technical requirements and offer practical commands. B is slightly better because it presents a clearer, unambiguous .NET 8/perfcollect recommendation, whereas A's opening dotnet-trace option muddles the distinction it subsequently explains.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Long-running intermittent issue with PerfView triggers
judgeRationales.rationale: B more directly and reliably addresses the requested unattended circular-buffer capture, especially the crucial trigger-on-symptom rationale. A is detailed and largely on target, but its extra possibly unsupported switches and less explicit recovery guidance reduce confidence.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on .NET Framework Windows
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide sound dump-based collection plans and A adds valuable continuous counters and root-cause analysis guidance. B more completely matches the requested diagnostic workflow by explicitly recommending a PerfView allocation trace, PerfView heap diffing, and collection before OOM.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Memory leak on Linux (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: A supplies a substantially more complete collection package for a slow Linux memory-growth investigation: OS RSS trend, runtime counters, repeated heap snapshots, environment/GC metadata, and a managed-versus-native triage path. B's allocation-trace recommendation is clearer and stronger, but its proposed data set omits the key ongoing memory/counter evidence and is less comprehensive. A does contain some overbroad wording about native diagnosis, so the advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Networking timeouts on Windows with admin (.NET 8)
judgeRationales.rationale: B closely follows the specified Windows/.NET diagnostic workflow with actionable PerfView commands, the required providers, and event-level analysis guidance. A is generally useful but answers with a different tooling plan and omits the rubric's key PerfView and RequestFailed details.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Slow requests on Windows with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: Both identify the central diagnostic technique correctly, but B better fulfills the requested collection guidance by including and explaining BufferSizeMB and CircularMB and by making manual stopping the default.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows container high CPU with PerfView
judgeRationales.rationale: B addresses the requested Windows-host/container tracing path comprehensively and satisfies every stated rubric item. A offers a plausible generic in-container dotnet-trace alternative, but misses the central host-admin PerfView workflow and symbol-handling guidance.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Windows modern .NET with admin high CPU
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly fulfills all three requested elements: it selects PerfView as preferred, gives an actionable collection command, and explains opening the ETL ZIP in CPU Stacks. A is generally useful but chooses the wrong primary tool under this task's stated Windows/admin conditions and omits the requested PerfView command.

judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the essential correct NativeAOT configuration: full-dump type 4 and the supplied createdump executable path. A's incorrect dump type and likely incorrect tool-path form would make its proposed configuration unsuitable, despite otherwise useful Kubernetes operational notes.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds branched Replace chain in format string manipulation

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds hot-path allocations in string humanization
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every requested rubric point, adds useful positive findings and prioritization, and is generally more concrete. It does include a few lower-value or debatable ancillary claims, but these do not outweigh its broader and more complete core analysis. A covers the major issues well but misses the requested recognition of existing allocation-conscious Concat helpers and includes a questionable whitespace-regex recommendation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Finds per-call Dictionary allocation not hoisted to static

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Flags Span inconsistencies and compound method chains in truncation library
